title: Constitution of the Republic of Singapore (Amendment) Bill
what_it_is: Constitution of the Republic of Singapore (Amendment) Bill

sections.label: Constitutional amendment for Parliament continuity
sections.summary: The Government proposes amending the Constitution to create a mechanism for Parliament's continuity during crises.

sentences.speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: The Government is therefore proposing to amend the Constitution to put in place a mechanism for the continuity of Parliament even during such moments of crisis.

sections.label: Parliament meeting across multiple places
sections.summary: Parliament will be able to meet with Members in two or more places appointed by the President, in contemporaneous communication.

sentences.speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: Instead, Parliament will be able to meet with Members spread across two or more places appointed by the President and in contemporaneous communication with each other.

sections.label: Six-month mechanism duration
sections.summary: The mechanism will be active for six months after the Bill is enacted and comes into force.

sentences.speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: The mechanism will be active for six months after this Bill is enacted and comes into force.

sections.label: Technology enables remote parliamentary functions
sections.summary: Technology has advanced so Parliament's functions, notably Chamber debates and committee proceedings, can be conducted remotely without great loss of quality.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Fortunately, technology has advanced today to the point where many of the functions of Parliament, most notably Chamber debates and official proceedings of committees, can be conducted remotely without any great loss of quality.

sections.label: Limitations of meeting at multiple sites
sections.summary: In-person discussions build trust and relationships, so in accepting multi-site technological meetings, limitations must be recognised and overcome.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The discussions that we have in person, in the grounds of Parliament, whether by design or by accident, form an important basis for trust, relationship building and even national decision-making.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: So, in accepting the necessity for Parliament, from time to time, to meet at multiple sites using technology, we must be aware what the limitations are, and think actively about ways to overcome them.

sections.label: Technology cannot replace human connections
sections.summary: Parliamentary work is done offline and online, but technology cannot replace face-to-face trust and relationship building.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Of course, democratic accountability holds that the business of Parliament should be as public as possible.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: But that does not change the fact that parliamentary work is done, offline and online, and technology can help, but cannot replace, the need to form human connections in doing this work.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The most important work of trust and relationship building in the service of the country is still done face to face, in Parliament and outside it.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Even though technology now allows us to see someone virtually, we still need to build that element of trust first.

sections.label: Bill empowers majority of Members
sections.summary: The Bill empowers the majority of Members to give notice that it is or will be impossible, unsafe or inexpedient for Parliament to sit and meet in one place.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The Bill empowers the majority of Members to give notice that "it is or will be impossible, unsafe or inexpedient for Parliament to sit and meet in one place".

sections.label: Workers' Party supports Bill
sections.summary: The Workers' Party supports the Bill, and a Member asks whether it would allow Parliament to adopt a video-conferencing approach with members calling in from home.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: In that light, the Workers' Party supports the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The language of the new Article 64A(2) reads that continuity arrangements "may be made for Parliament and its committees to sit, meet and despatch business with Members of Parliament being present at two or more appointed places and in contemporaneous communication with one another." Notwithstanding the advice from the Leader of the House in her letter of 27 April that the Government does not wish to adopt this approach right now, would this Bill thus allow Parliament to adopt the UK's video-conferencing approach or something similar, if it deems necessary to do so, with members calling in from home?

sections.label: Public right to live stream
sections.summary: The Member argues the public has the right to see a live stream of Parliament even if demand is low, and that continuity arrangements provide a good opportunity to proceed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: To be sure, even if demand is low, and provided that the cost is not prohibitive, which it is unlikely to be, I would still argue that the members of the public have the right to see live stream of parliament, even if only a minority choose to exercise that right at any given point in time.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Live streaming of parliament is common in other developed countries.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: But having said that, continuity arrangements would provide a good opportunity to proceed with this for the reasons that I have mentioned.

sections.label: Expanding public gallery online
sections.summary: The Member proposes expanding the notion of the public gallery online through live-streaming to ensure continuity of access, calling it an imperative in COVID-19 times.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: How can we ensure continuity of this access to live proceedings?

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I would propose that we expand the notion of the public gallery online through live-streaming to ensure continuity of access.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This may have been seen as a “nice to have” in the past but I would argue that in these COVID-19 times, this is now an imperative.

sections.label: Live streaming and archives mainstream
sections.summary: The Member says live streaming and maintaining archives are mainstream technologies so cost is no longer an obstacle, and quotes the Speaker on citizen participation.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Live streaming and maintaining archives are now mainstream technologies such that cost is no longer an obstacle. “I firmly believe that given our greater appetite for self-information in this digital age, we can nudge greater citizen participation by offering official channels they can trust,” these are not my words but yours, Mr Speaker.

sections.label: Live streaming and remote meeting clarifications
sections.summary: The Member asks the Minister to clarify whether live streaming will be part of continuity planning for public access and why the Bill does not provide for Parliament to meet remotely.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It must be made on a matter of principle, the same way that the Hansard and public gallery are manifestations of the democratic principle.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: So, will the Minister please clarify whether live streaming will be part of the continuity planning for public access to protect the integrity of our parliamentary process, especially with the public gallery closed to the electorate?

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Before I conclude, Mr Speaker, I would also like to ask the Minister to clarify why the Bill does not provide for Parliament to meet remotely under the new Article 64A should such need arise so that we do not have to keep tabling urgent amendments, since experts have shared that COVID-19 would not be the last pandemic.

sections.label: Support for the Bill
sections.summary: The speaker supports the Bill despite earlier suggestions and clarifications.

sentences.speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Notwithstanding my suggestions and clarifications above, I support the Bill.

sections.label: Urgent Constitutional Amendment Bill tabled
sections.summary: A Constitutional (Amendment) Bill is tabled and read under a certificate of urgency to put in place a continuity plan.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Today, we are tabling and reading a Constitutional (Amendment) Bill under a certificate of urgency to put in place a continuity plan.

sections.label: Proposed Article 64A(1)(a) arrangements
sections.summary: Proposed Article 64A(1)(a) sets out three situations allowing an alternative arrangement, including six months after Gazette publication.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Coming back to the provisions of this Bill, the proposed Article 64A(1)(a) specifies that the suggested alternative arrangement may be possible – one, for a period of six months after the date the Act is published in the Gazette; two, for a period of six months if Parliament resolves that it is or will be impossible, unsafe or inexpedient for Parliament to sit and meet in one place; or three, the Speaker presents to Parliament a notice in writing given by the majority of all Members of Parliament stating words to the same effect.

sections.label: Questions on inexpedient and majority threshold
sections.summary: The speaker asks the Leader of the House to elaborate on what inexpedient might look like and the reason for a majority threshold.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: In light of this, could the Leader of the House elaborate on what “inexpedient” might look like and what is the reason for setting the threshold for agreement to that of a majority through a resolution for future instances instead of, say two-thirds majority of elected members, as is the requirement today.

sections.label: Principles for Article 64A(2)(c)
sections.summary: The speaker asks the Leader of the House to elaborate on principles and concerns guiding arrangements under proposed Article 64A(2)(c).

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: For the benefit of this Parliament and future parliaments, would the Leader of the House elaborate on some principles and concerns that may guide arrangements mentioned in the proposed Article 64A(2)(c) both in the present as well as in the future?

sections.label: Summary and support for Bill
sections.summary: The Bill allows Parliament to keep sitting when it is impossible, unsafe or inexpedient to sit in one physical location, and the speaker supports it.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: In summary, this Bill puts in place measures which allow us to continue sitting as Parliament despite it being impossible, unsafe or inexpedient to sit at one, single physical location.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: On the basis that the provisions should be invoked sparingly and only when necessary, I support this Bill.

sections.label: Simple majority activation question
sections.summary: A question asks why activating continuity arrangements requires only a simple majority.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: Second, why does it only take a simple majority to activate continuity arrangements?

sections.label: Activation for future crises
sections.summary: Ms Anthea Ong asked whether the mechanism can be activated for future crises, and the answer is yes.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: Ms Anthea Ong asked whether the mechanism can be activated for future crises and the answer is yes.

sections.label: Public access to proceedings
sections.summary: The public will continue to have access to proceedings as they currently do when Parliament sits in this Chamber.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: The public will continue to have access to the proceedings as they currently do when Parliament sits in this Chamber.

sections.label: Highlights and activation conditions
sections.summary: Parliamentary highlights are loaded onto the microsite within three hours of broadcast, and continuity arrangements activate when sitting in one place may be unsafe.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: Parliamentary highlights are loaded onto this microsite within three hours of broadcast.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: The continuity arrangements will be activated when it is deemed that it may be unsafe for Parliament to sit in one place.

sections.label: Continuity of Parliament mechanism
sections.summary: The Bill's amendments put in place a mechanism to ensure Parliament's continuity in crisis so its business continues unhindered.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: The amendments in this Bill seek to put in place a mechanism to ensure the continuity of Parliament even in moments of crisis, so that the business of Parliament can continue unhindered.
